title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 89–90

units.title: Unit 89 — Expressions with do and make
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 184–185 (PDF pages 185–186).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish the common phrasal-verb meanings of do and make, including separable and inseparable patterns.
Recognise meaning shifts in do up, make up, make out and make for from clear contexts.
Choose do for common activities and duties, and make for outcomes, actions and established phrases without overgeneralising.
Use verb–noun collocations naturally, including do your best, make allowances for and make a go of something.

items.example: We can do without the printer until the replacement arrives.
items.note: Do without something means manage despite not having it.

items.example: The council wants to do away with unnecessary paperwork.
items.note: Do away with something means abolish or get rid of it.

items.example: After lunch, we made for the railway station.
items.note: Here make for means move towards a place.

items.example: What do you make of the manager's proposal?
items.note: Commonly used in questions about someone's judgement or interpretation.

items.example: The intruder made off when the alarm began to ring.
items.note: Intransitive phrasal verb meaning leave hurriedly, often to escape.

items.example: The flexible hours make up for the longer commute.
items.note: Make up for something means compensate for a disadvantage or loss.

items.section: B · Different meanings of do up
items.example: Please do up your coat before going into the cold.
items.note: With clothes or fastenings, do up means fasten or close something.

items.section: B · Different meanings of do up
items.example: They spent the spring doing up their kitchen.
items.note: With rooms or buildings, do up means renovate or improve.

items.section: B · Different meanings of do up
items.example: She did up the letters in brown paper and string.
items.note: With parcels or bundles, do up means wrap or tie together.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make out
items.example: In the fog, I could barely make out the lighthouse.
items.note: Often with can or could, make out can mean see something with difficulty.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make out
items.example: I can't make out why the system keeps restarting.
items.note: Often used with can/could plus a negative to mean understand or work out.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make out
items.example: He made out that the decision had been entirely his.
items.note: Make out that introduces a claim which may be misleading or untrue.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: Five smaller teams make up the engineering department.
items.note: Active use meaning form or constitute a whole.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: The panel is made up of experts from several countries.
items.note: Passive pattern be made up of plus the parts that constitute a whole.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: She made up a story to explain the missing key.
items.note: Here make up means invent something, often an excuse or story.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: She made herself up for the stage performance.
items.note: In the cosmetic sense, make somebody up means apply make-up.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: The pharmacist made up the prescribed cream.
items.note: Make up can mean prepare something by combining ingredients.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: Two volunteers joined us to make up the numbers.
items.note: To bring a group up to the number needed; also used for someone who merely fills a place.

items.section: B · Different meanings of make up
items.example: The pharmacist can make up your prescription this afternoon.
items.note: Pharmaceutical use of make up means prepare or dispense what was prescribed.

items.example: The thieves made off with several valuable paintings.
items.note: Make off with something means escape while taking it, usually dishonestly.

items.example: Clear instructions make for fewer mistakes.
items.note: A second meaning of make for: lead to or help produce a particular result.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: I usually do my homework before dinner.
items.note: Say do homework, not make homework.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: We divide the housework between us.
items.note: A household activity, commonly used with do.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: She likes to do some gardening on Sunday mornings.
items.note: Do gardening refers to the activity rather than a finished product.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: He tries to do exercise every morning.
items.note: Do exercise is a natural general collocation; exercise can be uncountable.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: I'll do the washing-up if you cook dinner.
items.note: British English expression; US English often says do the dishes.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: Just do your best during the interview.
items.note: Do one's best means make the greatest reasonable effort.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: I usually do the shopping on Friday evenings.
items.note: Use do for the activity of buying regular necessities.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: He does most of the cooking in their flat.
items.note: Means take responsibility for preparing meals.

items.section: C · Do collocations: activities and duties
items.example: Our firm does business with suppliers across Europe.
items.note: Do business with somebody means have commercial dealings with them.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: I'll make a cup of tea before the meeting.
items.note: Use make for preparing a drink.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: We need to make arrangements for the visiting researchers.
items.note: Often make arrangements for something or to do something.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The two organisations made an agreement to share equipment.
items.note: An agreement is something the parties reach or make, not do.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: Can I make a suggestion about the test procedure?
items.note: Say make a suggestion, not do a suggestion.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: We must make a decision before the deadline.
items.note: Make a decision is the standard verb–noun collocation.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The leaders feared that the neighbouring countries might make war.
items.note: Established expression, though wage war is also common.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The team made an attempt to restart the system.
items.note: Usually make an attempt to do something.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: I need to make a phone call before we leave.
items.note: Use make a call; not do a call in this context.

items.pt: tirar o melhor proveito de uma situação
items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The weather was poor, but we made the best of it.
items.note: Accept a difficult situation and get the best possible outcome.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: She made an effort to speak English throughout the meeting.
items.note: Common pattern: make an effort to do something.

items.pt: dar uma desculpa; inventar uma justificativa
items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: He made an excuse for arriving late.
items.note: Also make excuses; not do an excuse.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: Everyone makes a mistake occasionally.
items.note: Use make a mistake, not do a mistake.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The company made a profit despite rising costs.
items.note: Profit is an outcome, so the standard verb is make.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The business made a loss in its first year.
items.note: British English commonly says make a loss.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The couple wanted some privacy to make love.
items.note: An intimate expression; meaning depends on context and historical usage.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: Make the most of your time at the conference.
items.note: Use make the most of an opportunity, resource or situation.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The fan makes a strange noise when it starts.
items.note: Use make a noise or make noise, not do a noise.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: A clear presentation can make a good impression on employers.
items.note: Make an impression on somebody; good or bad are possible.

items.pt: fazer algo dar certo; ter sucesso em algo
items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: She worked hard to make a success of her small business.
items.note: Make a success of something means cause it to be successful.

items.pt: levar em consideração; ser compreensivo com
items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: We should make allowances for his lack of experience.
items.note: Take circumstances into account rather than judging too harshly.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: He made a gesture towards the empty chair.
items.note: A movement or symbolic action is something one makes.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: The child made a face when she tasted the medicine.
items.note: Make a face means produce a facial expression, usually of dislike or amusement.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: It's unkind to make fun of someone else's accent.
items.note: Make fun of somebody means mock them.

items.pt: dar muita atenção e carinho a
items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: Her grandparents always make a fuss of her when she visits.
items.note: British expression meaning give someone extra affection and attention.

items.section: C · Make collocations: results and actions
items.example: They were determined to make a go of their new café.
items.note: Informal expression meaning make an attempt or undertaking succeed.

sectionsChecked: A: Phrasal verbs with do and make
C: Collocations with do and make

units.title: Unit 90 — Expressions with bring and take
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 186–187 (PDF pages 187–188).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Phrasal verbs, idioms and verb patterns
learningObjectives: Use bring and take phrasal verbs with the right particles, objects and meaning in context.
Distinguish major polysemous senses of take in, take off, take on, bring down and related verbs.
Use established expressions such as bring to light, take into account and take for granted accurately.
Recognise informal phrasal verbs and their more formal equivalents when appropriate.

items.example: Her grandparents brought her up in a small village.
items.note: Bring someone up means raise them from childhood.

items.example: The organisers brought off an ambitious international event.
items.note: Bring something off means succeed in doing a difficult thing.

items.example: The dusty air brought on an attack of coughing.
items.note: Bring on can mean cause an illness, symptom or event to begin.

items.example: The new policy brought about major changes at work.
items.note: Bring about something means cause it to happen.

items.example: The publisher will bring out a new dictionary next spring.
items.note: For products, publications or models, bring out means introduce or release.

items.example: The school plans to bring back its annual science fair.
items.note: Reintroduce something that existed before.

items.example: New technology helped bring down manufacturing costs.
items.note: With prices, taxes or costs, bring down means lower.

items.example: The scandal could bring down the administration.
items.note: With governments or powerful people, bring down means cause to lose power.

items.example: We eventually brought her round to our point of view.
items.note: British English: bring somebody round to something, persuade them to agree.

items.example: My brother takes after our mother in both looks and character.
items.note: Take after someone means resemble a family member.

items.pt: retirar o que disse; voltar atrás
items.example: I wish I could take back that rude comment.
items.note: Take back words means withdraw a statement or apology-worthy remark.

items.example: There was too much information to take in at once.
items.note: Take something in means absorb or understand information.

items.example: Several customers were taken in by the fake reviews.
items.note: Take someone in means deceive them; often used in the passive.

items.example: Demand for the product took off after the launch.
items.note: For sales or careers, take off means become successful rapidly.

items.example: Our flight took off just after sunrise.
items.note: For aircraft, take off means leave the ground.

items.example: He can take off the head teacher's voice perfectly.
items.note: Informal British usage meaning imitate a person, often humorously.

items.example: The laboratory is taking on three technicians.
items.note: Take on staff means employ new people.

items.example: Don't take on more work than you can finish.
items.note: Take on a task means accept responsibility for it.

items.example: Amira will take over as project manager in November.
items.note: Take over as somebody means begin doing that person's role.

items.example: I took to my new teammates on the first day.
items.note: Take to somebody means start liking them, often straight away.

items.example: She took up swimming after moving to the coast.
items.note: Take up a hobby or sport means start doing it regularly.

items.example: The new safety rules will be brought into force in January.
items.note: A law or regulation is brought into force when it starts to apply.

items.example: The investigation brought several overlooked errors to light.
items.note: Reveal something that had been hidden or unknown.

items.example: The missed deadline brought tensions in the team to a head.
items.note: A crisis develops to a point where it must be addressed.

items.example: The meeting helped bring the disagreement into the open.
items.note: Make information or problems public instead of hiding them.

items.example: Supportive managers can bring out the best in their teams.
items.note: Help someone show their most positive qualities or abilities.

items.example: The dishonest seller took advantage of the customer's inexperience.
items.note: Can mean exploit unfairly; in other contexts it can mean use an opportunity well.

items.pt: não dar valor a; considerar garantido
items.example: Don't take the help of your colleagues for granted.
items.note: Here take someone or something for granted means fail to appreciate them.

items.example: I took it for granted that the meeting would be online.
items.note: Take it for granted that introduces an assumption.

items.example: The new supervisor took control of the situation.
items.note: Begin directing or organising something.

items.example: The view across the mountains took my breath away.
items.note: Often means surprise or impress very strongly.

items.example: The workshop takes place on Thursday afternoon.
items.note: Take place is used for an event happening at a specific time or location.

items.example: Starting the business was a risk, but she chose to take it.
items.note: Take a risk means deliberately do something with an uncertain outcome.

items.example: We must take the warning seriously.
items.note: Treat a person, topic or idea as important or worthy of consideration.

items.example: Please take maintenance costs into account when choosing the device.
items.note: Take something into account means include it in your decision or judgement.

items.example: She takes pride in the quality of her research.
items.note: Feel satisfaction in an achievement, activity or characteristic.

items.example: I took the opportunity to ask questions after the talk.
items.note: Typically followed by to plus infinitive: take the opportunity to do something.

items.example: We decided to take out insurance before travelling.
items.note: Take out insurance means arrange and purchase insurance cover.

items.example: Please take off your shoes before entering the studio.
items.note: A separate everyday sense of take off: remove clothing or accessories.

items.pt: adquirir o controle de uma empresa
items.example: A larger group plans to take over the local firm.
items.note: Take over can mean acquire control of an organisation.

items.example: Some cleaning products can bring on an allergic reaction.
items.note: Use bring on for something that triggers symptoms; an allergic reaction is more precise than an allergy attack.

sectionsChecked: C: Common expressions with bring and take
